title: Meet the Astronauts Who Spent 167 Days in Space!
summary: Have you ever dreamed of floating in space for almost half a year? Three real astronauts did just that! On June 1, NASA is hosting a special event where you can hear all about their adventure. The astronauts—Zena Cardman, Mike Fincke, and Kimiya Yui—spent 167 days on the International Space Station (ISS). That's like a giant science lab orbiting Earth! During their mission, they traveled a mind-blowing 71 million miles. That's like going around Earth 2,670 times! They did tons of experiments to help people on Earth and to get ready for future trips to the Moon and Mars. Mike Fincke is a space veteran—this was his fourth trip! He's now spent 549 days in space, which is one of the most for any NASA astronaut. For Zena Cardman, it was her very first spaceflight. The crew even celebrated 25 years of people living nonstop on the ISS. They splashed back down to Earth on January 15, landing in the ocean near San Diego. If you're in Washington, D.C., you can see them speak at NASA Headquarters at 11 a.m. on Monday. They'll share what it's like to live and work in space. It's a rare chance to hear from real-life space explorers!
why_it_matters: Knowing how astronauts live in space can help us imagine a future where people might visit Mars—maybe one day you could be one of them.

background_read: The International Space Station has been occupied continuously since 2000—that means for 25 years, there has never been an empty house in space!
NASA (the U.S. space agency) often works with space agencies from other countries, like Japan's JAXA, which sent astronaut Kimiya Yui.
Mike Fincke is one of the most experienced NASA astronauts; his total of 549 days in space is one of the longest records for an American.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA astronauts Zena Cardman, Mike Fincke, and Kimiya Yui, who recently returned to Earth.
WHAT: They spent 167 days on the ISS, traveled 71 million miles, and did science experiments.
WHERE: They lived on the ISS in orbit around Earth; the speak event is in Washington, D.C.
WHY: To share their space adventure and inspire future trips to the Moon and Mars.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled to hear first‑hand stories of floating in zero gravity and hope space travel becomes more common.
Some think space missions are very expensive and that the money could be used to solve problems here on Earth first.
They see the mission as a great chance to show how experiments in space lead to new medicines or better technology for everyone.
